blocks.path: Angina
s: Angina is a feeling of pain or tightness, usually in your chest.
It can be a sign of a heart problem, so it's important to see a GP as soon as possible if you think you may have it.

blocks.path: Angina > Symptoms of angina
s: The main symptom of angina is sudden pain in your chest, neck, shoulders, jaw or arms.

blocks.path: Angina > Symptoms of angina
s: The pain may:

blocks.path: Angina > Symptoms of angina
s: feel like tightness, squeezing or pressure, or like a dull ache

blocks.path: Angina > Symptoms of angina
s: make you feel sick, breathless, dizzy or sweaty

blocks.path: Angina > Symptoms of angina
s: These symptoms may be called an angina attack, episode or pain.

blocks.path: Angina > Symptoms of angina
s: They are often brought on by exercise, stress, emotion or cold temperatures – although sometimes there's no obvious trigger.

blocks.path: Angina > Symptoms of angina
s: Angina attacks usually last less than 10 minutes and should stop after resting for a few minutes or taking your angina medicine.

blocks.path: Angina > How to treat an angina attack
s: If you've been diagnosed with angina and get chest pain, follow the instructions you've been given for treating your angina:

blocks.path: Angina > How to treat an angina attack
s: Stop what you're doing and rest.

blocks.path: Angina > How to treat an angina attack
s: Use any medicine you've been prescribed – this is usually glyceryl trinitrate (GTN).

blocks.path: Angina > How to treat an angina attack
s: Take another dose after 5 minutes if the first dose does not help.

blocks.path: Angina > How to treat an angina attack
s: If you still have symptoms 5 minutes after taking the 2nd dose, call 999 for an ambulance.

blocks.path: Angina > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
s: you've been diagnosed with angina and have chest pain that does not stop after resting for a few minutes or after taking your angina medicine

blocks.path: Angina > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
s: you get sudden pain or discomfort in your chest that does not go away – the pain can feel like squeezing or pressure inside your chest, burning or indigestion

blocks.path: Angina > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
s: you get pain that spreads to your left or right arm, or your neck, jaw, shoulder, stomach or back

blocks.path: Angina > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
s: you have chest pain and you feel sweaty, sick, light-headed or short of breath

blocks.path: Angina > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
s: You could be having a heart attack.
Call 999 straight away as you need immediate treatment in hospital.

blocks.path: Angina > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
s: Do not drive yourself to A&E.

blocks.path: Angina > Immediate action required: Call 999 now if:
s: The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

blocks.path: Angina > Urgent advice: Get help from NHS 111 if:
s: you have chest pain or other symptoms of angina that come and go

blocks.path: Angina > Urgent advice: Get help from NHS 111 if:
s: you've been diagnosed with angina and it feels worse than before, is happening more often, lasts longer or happens when you're resting

blocks.path: Angina > Urgent advice: Get help from NHS 111 if:
s: You can call 111 or get help from 111 online.

blocks.path: Angina > What happens at your GP appointment
s: If a GP thinks you may have angina, you'll be referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist).

blocks.path: Angina > What happens at your GP appointment
s: You may have tests including:

blocks.path: Angina > What happens at your GP appointment
s: blood tests

blocks.path: Angina > What happens at your GP appointment
s: an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the electrical activity of your heart

blocks.path: Angina > What happens at your GP appointment
s: checking the level of oxygen in your blood

blocks.path: Angina > What happens at your GP appointment
s: scans, such as an angiogram, MRI scan or CT scan

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: Angina happens when the heart does not get enough blood.

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: This is usually due to coronary heart disease, where the blood vessels supplying blood to the heart become narrowed or blocked by fatty deposits.

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: But it can also be caused by the blood vessels in your heart tightening when they should not (vasospastic angina or microvascular angina).

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: You're more likely to get angina if you:

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: are a man aged 45 or over, or a woman aged 55 or over

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: smoke

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: drink more than 14 units of alcohol a week

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: are living with obesity or overweight

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: have high blood pressure or high cholesterol

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: have had heart problems before, like a heart attack or heart rhythm problem (arrhythmia)

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: have close relatives who have heart problems

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: have another condition, such as diabetes, arthritis or kidney disease

blocks.path: Angina > Causes of angina
s: British Heart Foundation has more information about vasospastic angina and microvascular angina.

blocks.path: Angina > Treatment for angina
s: If you have angina, you may be given medicine to:

blocks.path: Angina > Treatment for angina
s: treat an angina attack if you have one (glyceryl trinitrate)

blocks.path: Angina > Treatment for angina
s: lower your chances of having an angina attack, such as beta blockers

blocks.path: Angina > Treatment for angina
s: reduce your risk of having a stroke or heart attack, such as low-dose aspirin or statins

blocks.path: Angina > Treatment for angina
s: Sometimes you may be recommended to have surgery to increase the blood flow to your heart (coronary angioplasty or a coronary artery bypass).

blocks.path: Angina > Things you can do to help prevent angina attacks
s: If you have angina, there are things you can do to help symptoms or reduce the chance of attacks.

blocks.path: Angina > Things you can do to help prevent angina attacks > Do avoid things that trigger your angina attacks as much as possible, like stress, cold temperatures or eating large meals always have your angina medicine with you – use it as you have been told by your doctor try to quit smoking, if you smoke try to keep to a healthy weight eat a balanced diet have the most active lifestyle your symptoms will allow try to cut down on alcohol if you drink more than 14 units a week Information: NHS help to get healthy
s: NHS Better Health has free tools and support to help you lose weight, quit smoking, drink less and get active.

blocks.path: Angina > Things you can do to help prevent angina attacks > Do avoid things that trigger your angina attacks as much as possible, like stress, cold temperatures or eating large meals always have your angina medicine with you – use it as you have been told by your doctor try to quit smoking, if you smoke try to keep to a healthy weight eat a balanced diet have the most active lifestyle your symptoms will allow try to cut down on alcohol if you drink more than 14 units a week Information: NHS help to get healthy

blocks.path: Angina > How angina affects your life
s: Having angina means you're at higher risk of having a heart attack or stroke.
It's important to treat it and make healthy lifestyle changes to reduce this risk.

blocks.path: Angina > How angina affects your life
s: With treatment, the symptoms should improve over time and may eventually stop.

blocks.path: Angina > How angina affects your life
s: If your symptoms are well controlled, angina will not usually have a big impact on your life.
You'll usually be able to continue with most things, including exercise and sex.

blocks.path: Angina > How angina affects your life
s: But angina may affect your work if you have a job that involves a lot of physical activity, or if you drive buses, coaches or lorries.

blocks.path: Angina > How angina affects your life
s: Your doctor will talk to you about any changes you may need to make, and whether you need to inform the DVLA about your condition.

blocks.path: Angina > How angina affects your life
s: It's also best to speak to your doctor before you take up a new activity or if you're worried about exercising.

blocks.path: Angina > How angina affects your life
s: You may also need to think about practical things like always carrying your angina medicine, having spare medicine available and making sure you have enough with you when travelling.
